claims.statement: Creatine (as creatine monohydrate) is not an FDA-approved drug. It is marketed in the U.S. as a dietary supplement and as a GRAS (generally recognized as safe) food ingredient via industry self-affirmation notice, and structure/function claims on its labeling (e.g., supports muscle strength) do not require FDA pre-market approval but must carry the standard FDA disclaimer and are only subject to post-market notification.

context.population: consumers of creatine dietary supplements and creatine-fortified foods in the U.S.
context.formulation: creatine monohydrate (e.g., Creapure) in powders, bars, drinks

A dietary supplement for which a truthful and non-misleading claim is made in accordance with section 403(r)(6) is not a drug solely because the label or labeling contains the claim.
This statement has not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. This product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.

reviewFlags: regulatory-status claim; confirm no subsequent FDA action (e.g., warning letters, NDI objections) at review time

claims.statement: Creatine functions in the phosphocreatine/ATP energy-shuttle system: it is phosphorylated to phosphocreatine, which reversibly donates a high-energy phosphate group to ADP (via creatine kinase) to regenerate ATP, supplying rapid energy for short-duration, high-intensity muscle contraction.

extractedEvidence.quote: Creatine functions as part of the cell's energy shuttle. The high energy phosphate group of ATP is transferred to creatine to form phosphocreatine...This reaction is reversibly catalyzed by creatine kinase.
extractedEvidence.pageOrSection: PubChem PUG-View compound record, pharmacology section

extractedEvidence.quote: An amino acid derivative that occurs in vertebrate tissues and in urine. In muscle tissue, creatine generally occurs as phosphocreatine. Creatine is excreted as creatinine in the urine.
helps generate ATP and thereby supplies the muscles with energy, particularly for short-term events

claims.statement: In healthy, resistance-training individuals, creatine monohydrate supplementation is supported by a large controlled-trial literature (synthesized in the ISSN position stand) as the most effective ergogenic nutritional supplement currently available for increasing high-intensity/repeated-sprint exercise capacity and lean body mass gained from training; NIH's fact sheet corroborates significant increases in strength and power for short-duration, high-intensity activity, while noting creatine appears ineffective for endurance-type sport.

context.population: healthy adults engaged in resistance/high-intensity training
context.useCase: exercise performance (strength, power, high-intensity intermittent exercise)

extractedEvidence.quote: creatine monohydrate is the most effective ergogenic nutritional supplement currently available to athletes
often significantly increases strength (e.g., for bench presses) and power (e.g., for cycling)
performance during repeated short bursts of high-intensity, intermittent activity, such as sprinting and weight lifting

reviewFlags: efficacy is specific to high-intensity/strength training contexts and should not be generalized to endurance performance

claims.statement: Human trial protocols summarized by NIH and the ISSN position stand commonly used a loading phase of approximately 20 g/day (5 g four times daily, or ~0.3 g/kg/day) for 5-7 days, followed by a maintenance phase of 3-5 g/day (up to 5-10 g/day in larger athletes); an alternative protocol used 3-6 g/day for 3-4 weeks without a loading phase. This describes trial dosing context only, not a use recommendation.

context.doseText: Loading: ~20 g/day (5 g x4) or 0.3 g/kg/day for 5-7 days; maintenance: 3-5 g/day (up to 5-10 g/day); alternative: 3-6 g/day for 3-4 weeks without loading (trial protocol; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: 20 g/day creatine monohydrate in four portions of 5 g
ingest 5 g of creatine monohydrate (or approximately 0.3 g/kg body weight) four times daily for 5-7 days
creatine stores can generally be maintained by ingesting 3-5 g/day

reviewFlags: dose-context claim must never be presented as a use/dosing recommendation

claims.statement: NIH's Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheet states creatine is considered safe for short-term use by healthy adults, and the ISSN position stand states short- and long-term supplementation (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) is safe and well-tolerated in healthy individuals; NIH notes reported side effects include water-retention-related weight gain, and anecdotal reports of nausea, diarrhea and related GI distress, muscle cramps, and heat intolerance.

extractedEvidence.quote: considered safe for short-term use by healthy adults
nausea, diarrhea and related gastrointestinal distress, muscle cramps, and heat intolerance
short and long-term supplementation (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) is safe and well-tolerated in healthy individuals

reviewFlags: adverse-effect list is largely anecdotal/case-level per NIH source language, not systematically quantified
style pass 2026-08-29: 'considered safe' language attributed explicitly in-line to the NIH ODS source per audit recommendation — this is the source's assessment, not BioStack's assurance.

claims.statement: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis found creatine supplementation is associated with a modest, transient increase in serum creatinine (attributed to metabolic turnover) without significant change in glomerular filtration rate (GFR), supporting that creatine is likely safe for kidney function in healthy individuals; the authors caution that elevated serum creatinine in supplement users should be interpreted carefully alongside more specific renal-function markers, and evidence in people with pre-existing kidney impairment is more limited.

context.population: healthy adults and mixed clinical populations studied in included trials

extractedEvidence.quote: Creatine supplementation is associated with a modest, transient increase in serum creatinine levels, likely due to metabolic turnover rather than renal impairment.
No significant changes were observed in GFR, suggesting preserved kidney function.
does not induce renal damage in the studied amounts and durations in individuals without prior kidney damage

reviewFlags: evidence base for people with pre-existing renal impairment is comparatively thin; do not extrapolate general-population safety to that group

claims.statement: A popular online claim holds that creatine supplementation causes hair loss by raising DHT. A 2025 randomized, placebo-controlled 12-week trial in resistance-trained males (creatine monohydrate 5 g/day vs. placebo, n=38 completers) directly measured hormones and hair-follicle health and found no group-by-time interaction for any hormone or hair-related outcome, providing direct controlled-trial evidence against this claim; it does not, however, rule out effects at higher doses, in other populations, or over longer durations than 12 weeks.

context.population: resistance-trained males, ages 18-40 (n=38 completers of 45 randomized)
context.doseText: 5 g/day for 12 weeks (trial protocol; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: Creatine is a widely used ergogenic aid that enhances muscle strength and lean mass. However, concerns have been raised about the potential role in promoting hair loss by increasing dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
There were no group-by-time interactions observed for any hormones or hair-related outcomes.
This study was the first to directly assess hair follicle health following creatine supplementation, providing strong evidence against the claim that creatine contributes to hair loss.

reviewFlags: single trial, 12-week duration, males only; not a definitive population-wide ruling-out of any hair-loss association

claims.statement: Online marketing and popular use often position creatine as a broadly beneficial supplement for essentially any athlete or exerciser, including endurance athletes and general wellness/cognitive use. The strongest human evidence (NIH fact sheet, ISSN position stand) specifically supports benefit for short-duration, high-intensity, intermittent exercise and resistance training, and NIH states creatine appears ineffective for endurance-type sport; broader claims of universal athletic or cognitive benefit are not equally supported by the same controlled-trial base.

context.population: general supplement-using public, including endurance athletes and non-strength-sport users
context.useCase: gap between broad online marketing claims and evidence scope

extractedEvidence.quote: performance during repeated short bursts of high-intensity, intermittent activity, such as sprinting and weight lifting

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: distinguish narrow, well-supported use case (high-intensity/resistance exercise) from broad marketing claims covering all sport types and non-exercise wellness/cognitive uses
cognitive/anti-aging marketing claims for creatine were not evaluated in this expansion pass and should be sourced separately if added

conflicts.summary: General-population renal safety data (no significant GFR change; transient creatinine rise) is drawn mainly from healthy individuals and mixed clinical populations; the FDA GRAS safety conclusion is explicitly scoped to 'individuals without prior kidney damage.' Safety in people with pre-existing kidney impairment is comparatively under-studied and should not be assumed equivalent.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

UNII and ChEMBL identifiers not yet resolved from structured databases; DrugBank UNII/CAS fields were behind an authentication wall and could not be verbatim-confirmed beyond the CAS number already cross-checked via PubChem.
